summary: The article, dated October 12, 2023, examines how reliance on local property taxes creates unequal school funding across U.S. districts, hurting teacher retention, facilities, and student outcomes in poorer areas. It proposes reforms including reducing property tax dependence, raising state and federal shares, targeted funding, school-based budgeting, transparency, and community and private partnerships. Examples from named districts, Sweden, Finland, and the New Horizon Foundation illustrate possible approaches.
one_line: An October 2023 article on how property-tax-based school funding creates inequity and which reforms, from state per-pupil standards to partnerships, could fix it.
key_facts: The article is dated October 12, 2023 and focuses on local education funding models and budget allocation in the United States.
Local education is typically funded by state funds, federal contributions, and local revenues, with property taxes playing a dominant role.
Districts with high-value real estate can spend more on schools than districts with lower property values.
Thompson School District, led by Superintendent Elizabeth Martinez, has significantly higher revenue per student than neighboring Parksville District, led by Superintendent Jim Egan.
Jim Egan said the system is "inherently divisive, creating pockets of educational wealth and poverty."

Underfunded districts struggle to attract and retain qualified teachers, maintain facilities, and offer advanced courses or extracurriculars; their students often score lower on standardized tests and have reduced college entry rates.
Sweden uses a school voucher system encouraging competition and equal opportunity, while Finland prioritizes equal funding regardless of geographical location.
Dr. Anita Rivera, an educational economist, suggested the state set a standard per-pupil funding amount so each child gets the same starting point.
Rivera said federal education funding tends to be more equitable because it does not rely on the socio-economic status of locally defined areas.
Riverbank Unified School District, under Superintendent Carlos Gomez, secured funding for ESL programs, and Gomez reported a marked improvement in students' abilities across the board.
School-based budgeting would give individual schools more control over spending, and publicly accessible budgets promote accountability and community engagement.
The New Horizon Foundation, a non-profit, collaborated with local tech companies to fund state-of-the-art technology labs in schools in economically challenged areas.
The article suggests sales or income taxes as alternative revenue sources to reduce reliance on property taxes.
The article states there is no one-size-fits-all solution and that reform will not happen overnight.
